snippet.title: Life in Bible Times, Explained
snippet.description:
What was daily life really like in the world of the Bible? Bible Unearthed explores the people, places, customs and discoveries behind the stories: tunnels dug through solid rock, ancient cities, everyday food, work, laws and beliefs.

Each illustrated episode tells you what the biblical text says, what historians and archaeologists have found, and what is still debated. We respect the Bible as an ancient text and we never present speculation as fact.

New illustrated history videos every week. Subscribe and dig in.

mostViewedPublicVideo.title: How Hezekiah Cut a River Through a Mountain
mostViewedPublicVideo.description:
An examination of the Siloam Tunnel, an ancient water system in Jerusalem. This video details the engineering behind King Hezekiah's project to secure the Gihon Spring, explores the archaeological evidence including the Siloam Inscription, and discusses scholarly debates regarding the tunnel's dating and construction methods.

Key Topics:
- Historical and Biblical context (2 Kings 20:20, 2 Chronicles 32:30).
- Engineering specifications: The 583-yard tunnel and its precise gradient.
- Scientific analysis: Radiocarbon and uranium-thorium dating.
- Ongoing academic debates on construction timelines and theories regarding navigation techniques.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siloam_tunnel
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siloam_inscription

mostViewedOverThreeMinutes.title: Hidden for 2,000 Years: Who Hid the Dead Sea Scrolls?
mostViewedOverThreeMinutes.description:
Imagine throwing a stone into a dark cave in the desert, and hearing something shatter inside.

What ancient texts state:
- The Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa a) preserves all sixty-six chapters of the Hebrew Book of Isaiah in the same sequence as the Masoretic version, but contains over 2,600 textual variants, scribal corrections, longer word spellings, and a unique structural division into two halves of 27 columns and 33 chapters each.
- The Copper Scroll (3Q15) is not a literary composition but an inventory of 64 underground caches, 63 of which detail enormous deposits of buried gold and silver (such as a single location containing 900 talents of silver), alongside tithe vessels, priestly vestments, and a reference to a duplicate copy with additional details.

What historians and archaeologists conclude:
- The discovery began between late 1946 and early 1947 when Ta'amireh Bedouin shepherds, including Muhammed edh-Dhib, found Cave 1 near Qumran after tossing a rock and hearing breaking pottery, retrieving intact jars containing ancient scrolls.
- After passing through the antiques dealer Kando and Archbishop Mar Samuel, several scrolls were advertised in the Wall Street Journal in June 1954 and purchased by Israeli archaeologist Yigael Yadin for $250,000 to be housed at the Shrine of the Book at the Israel Museum.
- Over 11 caves excavated between 1946/1947 and 1956 yielded 981 manuscripts dating primarily between the 3rd century BCE and the 1st century CE, an era supported by paleography, radiocarbon tests, and recovered bronze coins.
- Roland de Vaux's excavations at the nearby site of Khirbet Qumran uncovered stepped cisterns identified as ritual baths (miqva'ot), an assembly room interpreted as a refectory, and an upper-story chamber with inkwells identified as a scriptorium where manuscripts were copied.

What remains uncertain:
- Scholarly consensus has long linked the scrolls and settlement to the Essenes, but competing hypotheses argue the scrolls were authored by Jerusalem priests or other Jewish factions, or that Qumran functioned as a villa, fortress, or pottery facility.
- The precise historical nature and deposit of the Copper Scroll remain debated, including whether its vast metal treasures represent actual Second Temple reserves, Bar Kokhba revolt caches, or folklore, and its referenced companion document has never been found.
- The definitive motive for caching the manuscripts in the cliffs remains unproven, though scholars commonly theorize they were concealed for safekeeping during the turmoil of the First Jewish–Roman War.

Sources:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead_Sea_Scrolls
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaiah_Scroll
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copper_Scroll
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qumran
